newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - BOJ rate hike seen further down river.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - BOJ rate hike seen further down river.

text.p: Speculation that the Bank of Japan (BOJ) might tighten credit this summer coursed through currency markets this week, but a lot more water could pass under the bridge before the central bank boosts rates, a Reuters poll showed.
Indeed a senior BOJ official said on Wednesday the central bank has no plans for an immediate rate rise even though some groups in Japan have called for a hike.

The BOJ official discount rate (ODR) has remained at a rock-bottom 0.5 percent since September 1995 in order to rev up the economy and provide cheap funding to Japanese financial institutions burdened with bad real estate loans.
Japan's fiscal 1997 began April 1, 1997 and ends March 31, 1998.

The poll of 10 leading U.S. commercial banks and brokerage firms showed that six expected a hike in the ODR during the October-through-December period of fiscal 1997, three predicted an increase in the January-through-March period of Japan's same fiscal year, and one forecast a tightening after the release of the next BOJ quarterly "tankan" survey this July.
Six out of 10 predicted a 50-basis-point tightening when the BOJ finally moves, three expected a quarter point increase, and one forecast a rise of 15 basis points.

Ron Leven, a currency strategist at J.P. Morgan, said the firm expected the BOJ to first hike the ODR by 25 basis points in the January-through-March period of fiscal 1997, then tighten again by the same amount in the April-through-June period of the new 1998 fiscal year.
Leven said not until roughly that time will there be enough strength in the economy and banks to tolerate a rate hike.
"While the economy is recovering, the recovery is still very narrow," Leven said. "Outside the export sector, there's still not a whole lot of health in the economy."
The latest Japanese trade data highlighted the vigorous export sector as the trade surplus more than doubled in April from a year earlier to 831.48 billion yen ($7.23 billion).
But some analysts were uncertain about the outlook for domestic demand following the Japanese government's move to raise the consumption tax on April 1 to 5.0 percent from 3.0 percent.

Monetary policy has to remain accommodative in order to offset the turn to more restrictive fiscal policy and an anticipated further appreciation in the yen, said Kathleen Stephansen, a senior economist at Donaldson, Lufkin and Jenrette Securities Corp.
She noted that Japanese exporters generally became competitive at 100 to 105 yen per dollar, and she predicted the yen will appreciate to 110 per dollar.
The dollar was fetching around 114 yen in Wednesday afternoon trading.
"At 110, you would not assume that the export industry will be killed, but by the same token, activity is likely to slow relative to an exchange rate that is at 125," she said.
Stephansen forecast a 50 basis point increase in the January-through-March period of fiscal 1997.
Sandy Batten, international economist at Citibank, is another member of the 50-basis-point camp, but he expected the hike in the October-through-December period of fiscal 1997.
Batten deemed the BOJ's current stance "extremely accommodative."

Often, BOJ rate hike speculation has increased near the release of the central bank's "tankan" survey. The most recent survey released in April showed some improvement in the mood of corporate Japan but also highlighted insecurity about the future.
The upcoming "tankan", however, may paint a different picture.

The July "tankan" will confirm that the Japanese recovery is on a "very sound" footing, said William Sullivan, a senior vice president and director of money market research at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
He said the BOJ will likely collect evidence that the economy has withstood the hike in the consumption tax.
Sullivan also noted that pressure from senior citizens regarding pension earnings is so extreme that it favors higher rates.
Therefore, he predicted the BOJ will hike by 50 basis points after the release of the July "tankan" survey.
